facts.statement: Liopleurodon fossils date from the Middle Jurassic to the Late Jurassic, specifically from the Callovian to the Kimmeridgian stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Middle Jurassic to Late Jurassic (Callovian to Kimmeridgian),

facts.statement: The genus Liopleurodon was first described by Henri Émile Sauvage in 1873.
facts.quote: authority: Sauvage, 1873

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Liopleurodon is Liopleurodon ferox.
facts.quote: type_species: Liopleurodon ferox

facts.statement: Historically, Liopleurodon has been synonymized with Pliosaurus ferox, Pliosaurus pachydeirus, and Ischyrodon meriani.
facts.quote: synonyms: * Pliosaurus ferox (Sauvage, 1873) Lydekker, 1888 Pliosaurus pachydeirus Seeley, 1869 ?Ischyrodon meriani von Meyer, 1838

facts.statement: Liopleurodon possessed four flippers, a short tail, a long head, and a short neck, typical of pliosaurids.
facts.quote: Like other plesiosaurs, Liopleurodon has four flippers, a short tail, and, like most pliosaurids, a long head and a short neck.

facts.statement: Studies indicate Liopleurodon was an ambush predator that fed on fish, cephalopods, and other marine reptiles.
facts.quote: Various studies show that Liopleurodon would have been an ambush predator, feeding on fish, cephalopods and other marine reptiles.

facts.statement: A 1999 BBC documentary exaggerated the size of Liopleurodon, depicting it as reaching 25 meters in length.
facts.quote: In 1999, its size was greatly exaggerated in the BBC documentary series Walking with Dinosaurs, where it was depicted as reaching 25 m in length.

facts.statement: Based on attributed specimens, Liopleurodon likely ranged in size from 2.46 to 8.09 meters in length.
facts.quote: However, the different attributed specimens show that the animal could reach a size ranging from 2.46 to 8.09 m long.

facts.statement: The name Liopleurodon was coined by Henri Émile Sauvage in 1873.
facts.quote: The genus name Liopleurodon was coined by Henri Émile Sauvage in 1873.

facts.statement: The holotype tooth of Liopleurodon ferox was found in Le Wast near Boulogne-sur-Mer and is now housed in the Lille Natural History Museum.
facts.quote: The holotype tooth of Liopleurodon ferox was discovered in Le Wast, near Boulogne-sur-Mer, and is since numbered as BHN 3R 197 and stored in the Lille Natural History Museum.

facts.statement: A tooth from Charly, preserved at the Paris School of Mines, serves as the holotype for L. grossouvrei and measures 7 cm in length with a 5.5 cm crown.
facts.quote: Another tooth from Charly, since preserved at the Paris School of Mines, embodies the holotype of L. grossouvrei. This tooth is 7 cm long, with the crown measuring 5.5 cm.

facts.statement: Charles William Andrews described the anatomy of Liopleurodon specimens from the Leeds Collection in two volumes published in 1910 and 1913.
facts.quote: Charles William Andrews described the anatomy of the marine reptile specimens of the Leeds Collection acquired by the British Museum of Natural History in two volumes, the first published in 1910 and the second in 1913.

facts.statement: While some studies recognize L. pachydeirus, it is generally considered a junior synonym of L. ferox due to a lack of clear diagnostic features.
facts.quote: Although some studies still recognize L. pachydeirus, it is generally considered as a junior synonym of the type species due to the lack of a clear diagnosis.

facts.statement: Because the holotype of L. ferox is a single tooth with questionable features, recent studies recommend designating a neotype to preserve the species' validity.
facts.quote: As the holotype specimen of L. ferox consists of a single tooth with questionable distinguishing features, several recent studies recommend the designation a more complete neotype to preserve its validity.

facts.statement: Liopleurodon lived from the Callovian stage of the Middle Jurassic to the Kimmeridgian stage of the Late Jurassic, approximately 166 to 155 million years ago.
facts.quote: Liopleurodon (; meaning 'smooth-sided teeth') is an extinct genus of carnivorous pliosaurid plesiosaurs that lived from the Callovian stage of the Middle Jurassic to the Kimmeridgian stage of the Late Jurassic period (approximately 166 to 155 million years ago).

facts.statement: Fossils of Liopleurodon are mainly found in Europe, with one occurrence reported in Mexico.
facts.quote: Fossils attributed to Liopleurodon, including some skeletons, are mainly known from Europe, with one occurrence reported in Mexico.

facts.statement: In 1838, Hermann von Meyer named Ischyrodon meriani based on a large tooth from Callovian-aged rocks in Fricktal, Switzerland.
facts.quote: In 1838, Hermann von Meyer applied the name Ischyrodon meriani to a large tooth from possibly Callovian-aged rocks in Fricktal, Switzerland.

facts.statement: In 1869, Harry Govier Seeley named Pliosaurus pachydeirus based on the first 17 cervical vertebrae from the Oxford Clay Formation near Great Gransden.
facts.quote: In 1869, Harry Govier Seeley had applied the name Pliosaurus pachydeirus to a series of cervical (neck) vertebrae representing the first 17 in the neck from the Oxford Clay Formation near Great Gransden.

facts.statement: In 1905, John Frederick Blake described two teeth from Rushden, England, that were similar to other L. ferox specimens but came from older strata.
facts.quote: In 1905, John Frederick Blake described two teeth from Rushden, England, similar to those of other Liopleurodon ferox specimens, though from older strata than those from Peterborough.

facts.statement: In 1888, Richard Lydekker suggested that the neck described by Seeley likely belonged to Pliosaurus ferox.
facts.quote: Lydekker stated in 1888 that the neck described by Seeley probably belonged to Pliosaurus ferox.

facts.statement: Hermann Linder described specimens of Liopleurodon ferox in 1913.
facts.quote: Hermann Linder also described specimens of Liopleurodon ferox in 1913.

facts.statement: A poorly preserved partial skeleton of Liopleurodon ferox was excavated from the Oxford Clay of Fletton, England, and is now housed at the University of Tübingen.
facts.quote: One of these was a poorly preserved partial skeleton excavated from the Oxford Clay of Fletton, England, housed in Institut für Geowissenschaften, University of Tübingen.

facts.statement: Friedrich von Huene described a partial skeleton of Liopleurodon from the Ornatenton Formation in Swabia, Germany, in 1934.
facts.quote: In 1934, Friedrich von Huene described a partial skeleton from Swabia, Germany, in the Ornatenton Formation.

facts.statement: Alexandre Bigot assigned teeth from Calvados, northern France, to Liopleurodon ferox in 1938.
facts.quote: In 1938, Alexandre Bigot used Pliosaurus ferox as well, assigning some teeth known from Calvados, in the north of France.

facts.statement: In 2024, Nikolay Zverkov and colleagues documented Liopleurodon ferox fossils from twenty-eight localities across European Russia.
facts.quote: In 2024, Nikolay Zverkov and colleagues documented numerous Callovian marine reptile fossils collected over nearly a century of fieldwork from twenty-eight localities across European Russia.

facts.statement: Specimens of Liopleurodon ferox were found in the Unzha River north of Makaryev and in a quarry in the Mikhaylovsky District.
facts.quote: The latter specimen, together with two of the teeth, was discovered in the Unzha River north of Makaryev, whereas the third tooth comes from a quarry in Mikhaylovsky District.

facts.statement: Peggy Vincent and colleagues described a partial postcranial skeleton of Liopleurodon found in 1979 in Saint-Laon, France, which dates to the Callovian.
facts.quote: Peggy Vincent and coauthors described a partial postcranial skeleton discovered in 1979 in a since-abandoned quarry in Saint-Laon, France, and also dated from the Callovian.

facts.statement: The Thouarsais specimen of Liopleurodon measures approximately 3.2 meters in its preserved state.
facts.quote: Informally nicknamed as the Thouarsais specimen, this fossil reach approximately 3.2 m in its preserved state.

facts.statement: Jair Israel Barrientos-Lara and colleagues described pliosaurid fossils near Tlaxiaco, Oaxaca, Mexico, in 2015.
facts.quote: In 2015, Jair Israel Barrientos-Lara and colleagues described two pliosaurid fossils found near the town of Tlaxiaco in Oaxaca, Mexico.

facts.statement: One fossil from the Kimmeridgian deposits of the Sabinal Formation in Mexico was attributed to Liopleurodon, but researchers deemed it too fragmentary for species-level identification.
facts.quote: These fossils were extracted from Kimmeridgian deposits in the Sabinal Formation, and one of them, the partial front end of a snout, was attributable to Liopleurodon, though the researchers considered the remains too fragmentary to provide a species-level identification.

facts.statement: In 2018, Davide Foffa and colleagues considered L. grossouvrei to potentially be a distinct genus based on its differences from P. andrewsi and L. ferox.
facts.quote: L. grossouvrei, although synonymized with "Pliosaurus" andrewsi by most authors, was considered to potentially be a distinct genus in its own right by Davide Foffa and colleagues in 2018, given its differences from "P." andrewsi and Liopleurodon ferox.

facts.statement: In 1960, Lambert Beverly Halstead considered Liopleurodon distinct from Pliosaurus based on major differences in their mandibles.
facts.quote: Lambert Beverly Halstead, then known as Tarlo, published a review of Upper Jurassic pliosaurid taxonomy in 1960. He considered Liopleurodon to be distinct from Pliosaurus, noting major differences between the mandibles of the two genera.

facts.statement: Espen Knutsen reassigned L. macromerus and L. rossicus to Pliosaurus in his 2012 revision of the genus.
facts.quote: Based on Noè's observations, Espen Knutsen reassigned both L. macromerus and L. rossicus to Pliosaurus in his 2012 revision of the genus.

facts.statement: In 2015, researchers attributed a partial snout fossil from Mexico to Liopleurodon but noted it was too fragmentary for species-level identification.
facts.quote: In 2015, Jair Israel Barrientos-Lara and colleagues described two pliosaurid fossils found near the town of Tlaxiaco in Oaxaca, Mexico. These fossils were extracted from Kimmeridgian deposits in the Sabinal Formation, and one of them, the partial front end of a snout, was attributable to Liopleurodon, though the researchers considered the remains too fragmentary to provide a species-level identification.

facts.statement: Sauvage described the animal that produced the holotype tooth of Liopleurodon ferox as having reached completely gigantic proportions in 1873.
facts.quote: In his original 1873 description, Sauvage noted that the holotype tooth of L. ferox came from an animal which, according to him, had reached "completely gigantic proportions".

facts.statement: Liopleurodon first gained public attention in 1999 through an episode of the BBC series Walking with Dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Liopleurodon first came to the public attention in 1999 when it was featured in an episode of the BBC television series Walking with Dinosaurs

facts.statement: A 2019 study re-identified a key vertebra previously thought to belong to Liopleurodon as actually coming from a sauropod dinosaur.
facts.quote: a 2019 study finally re-identified it as actually coming from a sauropod dinosaur

facts.statement: Estimates suggest the holotype tooth of Liopleurodon ferox belonged to an individual approximately 5.24 meters in total length.
facts.quote: According to their estimates, the holotype tooth of L. ferox belonged to an individual measuring approximately 5.24 m in total length

facts.statement: Sauvage did not assign the genus Liopleurodon to any specific reptile group when he established it in 1873.
facts.quote: When Sauvage established the genus Liopleurodon in 1873, he did not assign it to any particular group of reptiles

facts.statement: Sauvage recognized Liopleurodon as a plesiosaur in 1880, thirteen years after establishing the genus.
facts.quote: It was not until thirteen years later, in 1880, that he recognized it as a plesiosaur

facts.statement: Liopleurodon ferox has been classified within the family Pliosauridae since 1888, an assignment retained ever since.
facts.quote: Since L. ferox had been referred primarily to the type genus from 1888 onward, it was consequently classified within this group of marine reptiles, an assignment that has been retained ever since

facts.statement: In 2012, Benson and colleagues proposed that Pliosauridae is more closely related to Plesiosauroidea than to Rhomaleosauridae.
facts.quote: However, in 2012, Benson and colleagues recovered a different topology, with Pliosauridae being more closely related to Plesiosauroidea than Rhomaleosauridae

facts.statement: Studies using swimming robots suggest that Liopleurodon's flipper-based propulsion provided good acceleration, a desirable trait for an ambush predator.
facts.quote: A study involving a swimming robot has demonstrated that although this form of propulsion is not especially efficient, it provides very good acceleration—a desirable trait in an ambush predator

facts.statement: Studies of the skull suggest Liopleurodon could scan the water with its nostrils to locate the source of smells.
facts.quote: Studies of the skull have shown that it could probably scan the water with its nostrils to ascertain the source of certain smells

facts.statement: There are currently only two known examples of Liopleurodon preserved with stomach contents.
facts.quote: Currently, there are only two known examples of a Liopleurodon preserved with stomach contents

facts.statement: One Liopleurodon specimen preserved stomach contents including at least seven gastroliths, numerous cephalopod hooklets, fish bones, and a reptile tooth.
facts.quote: The abdominal region preserves at least seven gastroliths, numerous teuthoid cephalopods hooklets, fish bones, and a single tooth that most likely belonged to a reptile

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Liopleurodon might have been an ambush predator, as its slow swimming speed makes hunting abundant squids unlikely unless it relied on ambush tactics.
facts.quote: One possibility is that Liopleurodon could have fed on food supplies that are abundant (i.e. squids), but considering that plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs were also abundant and that the plesiosaurs' swimming speed is likely very slow compared to squids, this interpretation may be unlikely unless Liopleurodon was an ambush predator

facts.statement: It is debated whether Liopleurodon was an opportunistic feeder, with cephalopod hooklets representing acid-resistant residues of a varied diet including vertebrate skeletal components.
facts.quote: Another possibility is that Liopleurodon may have been an opportunistic feeder, with cephalopod hooklets being representative of the acid resistant residue of its varied diet—skeletal components of various vertebrates that lost to the acid environment of the gut

facts.statement: A hypothesis suggests Liopleurodon fed on large cephalopod-feeders, but there is no firm evidence to support this claim.
facts.quote: The other possibility is that the pliosaur fed on large cephalopod-feeders, with the hooklets representing the residues of the stomach contents of the pliosaur's prey, but there is no firm evidence to this claim

facts.statement: Gastroliths found in Liopleurodon may have been swallowed accidentally or represent acid-resistant residue of carbonate-cemented sandstone.
facts.quote: It is therefore possible that the pliosaur swallowed them accidentally and that they remained in its stomach, or alternatively that they represent the acid-resistant residue of carbonate-cemented sandstone

facts.statement: Liopleurodon fossils are primarily found in Middle Jurassic deposits from Germany, England, France, and Russia.
facts.quote: Fossils attributed to Liopleurodon are primarily known from deposits dated to the Callovian stage of the Middle Jurassic in present-day Germany, England, France, and Russia.

facts.statement: The oldest known Liopleurodon fossil is a tooth crown from Germany dating to approximately 164.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: The oldest known occurrence of the genus is an isolated tooth crown discovered in a quarry near the German city of Hildesheim, dating to approximately 164.5 million years ago, i. e. lower Callovian.

facts.statement: The youngest known European Liopleurodon fossil dates to about 161.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: The youngest known European occurrence corresponds to the French holotype, recovered from upper Callovian strata dated to about 161.5 million years ago.

facts.statement: The epicontinental sea where Liopleurodon lived reached depths of up to approximately 100 meters in some areas.
facts.quote: This epicontinental sea reached depths of up to approximately 100 m in some areas.

facts.statement: The genus Liopleurodon was named by Sauvage in 1873.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Sauvage, 1873

facts.statement: Two species are recognized: L. ferox, named by Sauvage in 1873, and L. pachydeirus, named by Seeley in 1869.
facts.quote: subdivision: L. ferox Sauvage, 1873 (tipo) L. pachydeirus Seeley, 1869

facts.statement: The genus name Liopleurodon was coined by Henri-Émile Sauvage in 1873 based on three teeth measuring 70 millimeters.
facts.quote: El nombre del género Liopleurodon fue acuñado por Henri-Émile Sauvage en 1873 sobre la base de muy escasos restos consistentes de tres dientes de 70 milímetros.

facts.statement: A tooth found near Boulogne-sur-Mer, France, was named Liopleurodon ferox.
facts.quote: Un diente, hallado cerca de Boulogne-sur-Mer, Francia en capas que datan del Calloviense, fue nombrado Liopleurodon ferox

facts.statement: Only L. ferox is known from more or less complete skeletons.
facts.quote: Solo L. ferox es conocido de esqueletos más o menos completos.

facts.statement: Liopleurodon means "smooth-sided teeth" and is a large carnivorous marine reptile belonging to the short-necked plesiosaur clade Pliosauroidea.
facts.quote: Liopleurodon (nombre griego que significa «dientes de lados lisos») es un género de un gran reptil marino carnívoro perteneciente a los Pliosauroidea, un clado de plesiosaurios de cuello corto.

facts.statement: Two species of Liopleurodon lived from the Bathonian to the Kimmeridgian, between 166 and 155 million years ago.
facts.quote: Se han descrito dos especies de Liopleurodon, que vivieron desde la edad Bathoniense (en la época Jurásico Medio) hasta el Kimmeridgiense (en el Jurásico Superior), entre hace 166 a 155 millones de años.

facts.statement: Four strong fin-like limbs suggest that Liopleurodon was a powerful swimmer.
facts.quote: Cuatro fuertes miembros similares a aletas sugieren que Liopleurodon era un poderoso nadador.

facts.statement: A study using a swimming robot showed that Liopleurodon's propulsion method provided good acceleration, a desirable trait for an ambush predator.
facts.quote: Un estudio que utilizó un robot nadador ha demostrado que aunque de esta forma de propulsión no es especialmente eficiente, provee una muy buena aceleración - un rasgo deseable para un depredador de emboscada.

facts.statement: Skull studies suggest Liopleurodon likely scanned the water with its nostrils to detect certain smells.
facts.quote: Estudios del cráneo han mostrado que probablemente escudriñaba el agua con sus narinas para comprobar la fuente de ciertos olores.

facts.statement: The largest known L. ferox skull measures 1.54 meters in length.
facts.quote: El mayor cráneo conocido perteneciente a L. ferox mide 1,54 metros de largo.

facts.statement: An exceptionally well-preserved L. ferox skeleton measuring about 4.5 meters long is exhibited at the University of Tübingen in Germany.
facts.quote: Un esqueleto excepcionalmente bien preservado de L. ferox está en exhibición en el Institut und Museum für Geologie und Paläontologie de la Universidad de Tübingen en Alemania. Este espécimen mide cerca de 4,5 metros de largo.

facts.statement: An adult L. ferox may have averaged 5 to 7 meters in length.
facts.quote: Un L. ferox adulto pudo haber promediado 5 - 7 metros de largo.

facts.statement: A partial jaw measuring 2.8 meters long is exhibited at the University of Oxford's Natural History Museum, estimated to have a total length of over 3 meters.
facts.quote: Un espécimen parcial de una mandíbula que mide 2,8 metros de largo está en exhibición en el Museo de Historia Natural de la Universidad de Oxford: se estima que la longitud total de la mandíbula medía más de 3 metros.

facts.statement: Estimating the maximum size of Liopleurodon has been a controversial topic.
facts.quote: Estimar el tamaño máximo de Liopleurodon ha sido un tema controvertido.

facts.statement: The case of Kronosaurus has exposed uncertainty regarding the accuracy of Tarlo's suggestion for estimating plesiosaur sizes.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, el caso de Kronosaurus ha expuesto cierta incertidumbre acerca de la precisión de la sugerencia de Tarlo.

facts.statement: New research on plesiosaur anatomy casts further doubt on Tarlo's hypothesis, revealing that their skulls were typically only one-fifth of their total length.
facts.quote: Nueva investigación sobre la anatomía de los pliosaurios ha arrojado más dudas sobre la hipótesis de Tarlo para estimar el tamaño de los pliosaurios y revela que los cráneos de estos animales eran típicamente solo un quinto de la longitud total.

facts.statement: In 1999, Liopleurodon was depicted in a BBC Walking with Dinosaurs episode as a 25-meter-long animal.
facts.quote: En 1999, Liopleurodon fue representado en un episodio de la miniserie de televisión de la BBC Caminando con Dinosaurios, en la cual fue representado como un enorme animal de 25 metros de largo

facts.statement: Liopleurodon belongs to the family Pliosauridae, a clade within Plesiosauria that existed from the Jurassic to the Cretaceous in Europe and North America.

facts.statement: A 2013 analysis classified Liopleurodon, Simolestes, Peloneustes, Pliosaurus, and Brachaucheininae into a clade called Thalassophonea.

facts.statement: The time range for Liopleurodon is from the Callovian to the Berriasian, between 165.3 and 137.05 million years ago.

facts.statement: The parent group of Liopleurodon is Thalassophonea.

facts.statement: Liopleurodon belongs to the family Pliosauridae.

facts.statement: Liopleurodon is classified in the class Reptilia.

facts.statement: However, Knutsen et al. (2012) reclassified L. rossicus back into Pliosaurus.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, Knutsen et al (2012) lo han reclasificado nuevamente en Pliosaurus.

facts.statement: Some fossils from the Kimmeridge Clay Formation in England suggest a taxon over 15 meters long, but this specimen has not been assigned to the genus Liopleurodon.
facts.quote: Algunos restos fósiles excavados en la Formación Kimmeridge Clay en Inglaterra indican un taxón mucho mayor, posiblemente de más de 15 metros de largo. Sin embargo, este ejemplar no ha sido asignado al género Liopleurodon.

facts.statement: A specimen originally assigned to Stretosaurus macromerus is now thought to belong to Liopleurodon as L. macromerus, though it has more recently been reclassified as Pliosaurus macromerus.
facts.quote: Este espécimen fue originalmente asignado al género Stretosaurus (como Stretosaurus macromerus), pero actualmente se cree que pertenece al género Liopleurodon y ha sido renombrado L. macromerus. facts.statement: Liopleurodon was one of the superpredators of the Middle and Late Jurassic seas covering Europe.
facts.quote: Fue uno de los superdepredadores de los mares del Jurásico Medio y Superior que cubrían Europa.
